questions.prompt: Which of the following best defines a data element under ISO/IEC 11179?
options: Object class, property, and representation
Table, column, and data type
Name, definition, and owner
Business metadata, technical metadata, and operational metadata
Capture, store, and publish
Entity, attribute, and relationship
questions.explain: ISO/IEC 11179 builds a data element from object class (what real-world thing is being described, like 'Customer'), property (the specific characteristic, like 'Date of Birth'), and representation (how it's actually stored, like a DATE value). Together those three parts fully specify the data element in an unambiguous, comparable way.
questions.distractorExplain: Option F (entity, attribute, relationship) is the vocabulary of general data modeling, which sounds like a plausible match since data elements do describe entities' attributes. But ISO/IEC 11179 specifically defines its own three-part structure — object class, property, and representation — not these generic data-modeling terms.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about business, technical, and operational metadata, per Lesson 2.
options: Business metadata is the one of the three types that must be deliberately written by a person rather than generated automatically
Technical metadata is typically produced automatically by the database or system itself
Operational metadata describes things like when data was last loaded and how many rows were affected
A business user who only has business metadata can always tell whether today's number is fresh or three weeks stale
All three types are typically stored in the same single artifact: the business glossary
questions.explain: Business metadata must be deliberately written by a person, since it's the one type that doesn't generate itself; technical metadata (types, constraints) and operational metadata (load times, row counts) are both produced automatically by the system and by pipelines/schedulers respectively. A business user with only the business definition has no freshness information — that's operational metadata's job, which they lack. And the three types are stored in different places (the glossary, INFORMATION_SCHEMA/dictionary, job logs and dashboards), not one single artifact.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it actually is, per Chapter 1.
right: A system built to store, organize, and serve metadata, separate from the underlying data itself
Answers 'what is this, structurally?' — produced automatically by the database system
Answers 'what actually happened to this data?' — produced automatically by pipelines and schedulers
Answers 'what does this mean to the business?' — produced by stewards
questions.explain: Business metadata answers what a concept means to the business, produced by stewards. Technical metadata answers what something is structurally, produced automatically by the system. Operational metadata answers what actually happened to the data, produced automatically by pipelines. A metadata repository is a system built specifically to store and serve all of that, separate from the underlying data.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: of the five stages in the metadata lifecycle (capture, store, publish, maintain, retire), the ________ stage is the one most commonly skipped, because nothing visibly breaks the day an entry goes stale.
questions.explain: Lesson 4 names Maintain as the stage most programs skip — unlike Capture (needed to launch) or Publish (a hidden glossary is an obvious failure), nothing visibly breaks when an entry quietly goes stale, until someone eventually finds a clearly wrong definition and stops trusting the whole glossary.

questions.prompt: Put the five stages of the metadata management lifecycle in the correct order, per Lesson 4.
items: Capture — metadata gets created, either automatically or by a person
Store — it's recorded somewhere searchable, like a glossary or catalog
Publish — it's made visible to the people who need it
Maintain — it gets reviewed and updated as things change
Retire — the entry is marked retired when the thing it describes is deprecated
questions.explain: Lesson 4's five-stage lifecycle runs capture, store, publish, maintain, retire in that order, mirroring the data quality lifecycle. Maintain is the stage most often skipped, because nothing visibly breaks when it's neglected — metadata just quietly rots.

questions.prompt: A BI team adopts a catalog tool bundled with its reporting platform, the compliance team separately maintains its own glossary for regulatory terms, and a data engineering team tracks lineage in a third tool. Per Lesson 5, what problem does this create, and what is the long-term fix?
options: Metadata about the same table now lives in three unsynced places; the fix is a catalog that integrates with the existing tools rather than becoming a fourth standalone repository
No problem — as long as each team's tool is internally consistent, it doesn't matter that the tools don't talk to each other
The fix is for every team to switch to the exact same vendor's single tool, since integration across vendors is never possible
This is unavoidable and has no fix; metadata repository sprawl is simply a permanent cost of having multiple teams
questions.explain: Lesson 5 calls this repository sprawl — each tool is individually reasonable, but together they let metadata about the same object drift out of sync with no one keeping it aligned. Lesson 20 later explains the fix: a catalog that pulls from the existing glossary, dictionary, and lineage tools as an integration point, rather than becoming a fourth silo competing with them.

questions.prompt: A company's glossary term 'Customer Lifetime Value' is calculated from five different tables across two systems. Per Lesson 6, how many glossary entries should this concept have, and why?
options: Exactly one — a glossary is organized around business concepts, not around however many tables happen to implement them
Five — one entry per table the calculation touches, so every source is documented
Two — one entry per system involved in the calculation
None — concepts that span multiple tables don't belong in a glossary at all, only in the data dictionary
questions.explain: Lesson 6 is explicit that a glossary should be organized around the business concepts people actually talk about, not restated one table at a time. 'Customer Lifetime Value' stays exactly one glossary term with one agreed definition, no matter how many tables implement it underneath — that implementation detail belongs in the data dictionary instead.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about writing good glossary definitions, per Lesson 7.
options: 'Active Customer: a customer who is active' fails because it's circular — it restates the term using itself
A usable definition should state a threshold explicitly ('last 90 days') rather than a vague qualifier like 'recently'
Naming the exact column or query that calculates a concept makes a glossary definition stronger and more precise
A definition is self-contained if it's understandable without needing to already know the term or look up several other terms first
Vague qualifiers like 'significant' or 'typically' are acceptable as long as the rest of the sentence sounds confident
questions.explain: Lesson 7's four-part test requires specificity (explicit thresholds, not vague qualifiers like 'recently' or 'significant') and self-containment (no circular restating of the term, no needing to chase down other terms first). Naming a specific column or query is implementation leakage — exactly the trap the lesson warns against, not a strength; that detail belongs in the data dictionary.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a definition like 'Churn: when a customer churns' is an example of a ________ definition — one that only makes sense to someone who already understands the term.
questions.explain: Lesson 7 names this failure mode a circular definition — it restates the term using itself or a close synonym instead of describing the actual underlying behavior the term refers to.

questions.prompt: Match each stage of the glossary term lifecycle to what it means, per Lesson 8.
right: Submitted for approval, with the proposing steward's rationale attached
The official, current definition — the state most of a glossary should be in most of the time
Proposed but not yet reviewed, visible but flagged as unofficial
Retired, but kept visible and clearly marked rather than deleted, so historical references still resolve
questions.explain: Draft is proposed but unreviewed; In review is submitted for approval with rationale attached; Approved is the official current definition most terms should sit in; Deprecated is retired but kept visible and marked, not deleted, so historical references still resolve.

questions.prompt: A team wants to mark 'Customer' and 'Account' as synonyms in the glossary, since colloquially people use them interchangeably. Per Lesson 9, is this the right modeling choice?
options: No — a single customer might have multiple accounts (or an account might belong to multiple customers), so they're related terms, not true synonyms; marking them as synonyms would silently lose a real distinction
Yes — any two terms used interchangeably in casual conversation should always be marked as synonyms
No — 'Customer' and 'Account' can't be linked at all in a glossary, since only terms in the same hierarchy can be related
Yes, but only if both terms are also marked deprecated at the same time
questions.explain: Lesson 9 describes exactly this scenario as the synonym trap — 'Customer' and 'Account' are near-synonyms, not true synonyms, because the relationship between them (one customer can have multiple accounts) is a real distinction the business relies on. Collapsing them into a synonym pointing to one official term would lose that distinction; 'related term' is the honest relationship here.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building a business glossary in the correct order, per Lesson 10.
items: Pick one domain, not the whole organization
List the terms people actually argue about
Draft definitions using the four-part test
Route each draft through approval
Model relationships between terms as the term count grows
Publish and announce the glossary
questions.explain: Lesson 10's process scopes to one domain first, lists the terms causing real confusion, drafts definitions against the four-part test, routes them through approval before they become official, adds hierarchy/synonym/related-term relationships as the glossary grows, and finally publishes and announces it — skipping that last step leaves a glossary nobody knows exists.

questions.prompt: A developer runs INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS against dbo.Customer and sees that IsActiveFlag is a non-nullable BIT with a default of 0. Per Lesson 12, what can this query NOT tell them?
options: What the column actually means in business terms — that a customer is 'active' means they purchased in the last 90 days, recalculated nightly — since that's business context a person has to write
The column's data type
Whether the column allows NULL values
The column's default value
questions.explain: INFORMATION_SCHEMA gives structural facts automatically (type, nullability, default) with zero chance of being out of sync, since it reads the live schema. It cannot tell you what a column means in business terms — that's business metadata, which Lesson 2 established doesn't generate itself and has to be written by a person, typically attached via an extended property.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about data dictionary standards, per Lesson 13.
options: Even though INFORMATION_SCHEMA auto-generates structural fields, the consistency of what those fields actually say still has to be deliberately maintained
Every documented table and column should have a non-empty description, not just the ones someone got around to
If the glossary defines 'Active Customer' one way, dictionary descriptions that reference the concept should reuse that same wording rather than independently rephrasing it
A dictionary with 40% of its columns documented is already most of the way to being useful
Naming convention compliance has nothing to do with the data dictionary — that belongs entirely to Data Governance Foundations
questions.explain: Lesson 13 is explicit that auto-generation doesn't guarantee consistency — one table might use CustID, another customer_id. Naming compliance, mandatory description coverage, and consistent terminology (reusing the glossary's own wording) are all standards the dictionary has to enforce deliberately. A 40%-documented dictionary is explicitly called out as not 40% useful, since undocumented columns are exactly where confusion concentrates, and the dictionary is named as a good place to catch naming violations, not something unrelated to them.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a column that gets renamed, resized, or dropped while its dictionary entry still describes the old shape is an example of ________ drift — detectable automatically by comparing the live schema to the documentation.
questions.explain: Lesson 15 calls this structural drift, as distinct from descriptive drift (the schema stays the same but the business meaning quietly shifts). Structural drift is detectable automatically because INFORMATION_SCHEMA is always current and can be diffed against the documented schema.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it actually is, per Chapter 3.
right: A structured inventory of physical data structures — tables, columns, types, constraints
The system stored procedure used to attach a human-written description to a database object
A human-attachable metadata field, like a description, stored directly on a database object
Whether a column is allowed to contain no value
questions.explain: A data dictionary is the structured inventory of physical structures. Nullability is whether a column can be empty. An extended property is the human-attachable metadata field itself, like a description. sp_addextendedproperty is the stored procedure used to attach it to a database object.

questions.prompt: A ShippingStatus column was documented as having three values (Pending, Shipped, Delivered). A developer later adds a fourth value, Returned, to the application code without telling anyone, and the column's data type never changes. Per Lesson 15, would a structural-drift query catch this?
options: No — the schema itself (still a VARCHAR column) didn't change, so only a scheduled review checking actual distinct values against the documented ones would catch this descriptive drift
Yes — INFORMATION_SCHEMA would show the new VARCHAR length needed for 'Returned' and flag it automatically
Yes — any new value added to a column automatically triggers a dictionary update in SQL Server
No, and there is no way to ever catch this kind of drift, automated or manual
questions.explain: This is Lesson 15's worked example exactly — the schema (a VARCHAR column) never changed, so no automatic structural-drift query flags it. Only a scheduled review, where the accountable owner actually checks the current distinct values against the documented ones, would catch this kind of descriptive drift.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building a data dictionary in the correct order, per Lesson 14.
items: Pull the schema using INFORMATION_SCHEMA rather than starting from a blank page
Prioritize the tables people actually query
Write descriptions, enforcing naming, coverage, and terminology standards
Attach descriptions with extended properties
Link to the glossary wherever a column implements a business concept
Publish it somewhere searchable
questions.explain: Lesson 14's process starts from the real schema rather than guessing, prioritizes the most-used tables first, writes standards-compliant descriptions, attaches them with extended properties so they live with the database, links back to the glossary where relevant, and finally publishes the result somewhere searchable.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best defines a Critical Data Element (CDE)?
options: A data element whose accuracy, timeliness, or integrity has outsized consequences if it's wrong — for regulatory reporting, financial statements, or major business decisions
Any column that has been fully documented in the data dictionary with a non-empty description
Any element that appears in more than one table across the database
A column that is designated as a primary key or foreign key
Any data element a business steward personally considers important
A column whose name doesn't follow the organization's naming convention
questions.explain: Lesson 16 defines a CDE as a data element whose error has outsized consequences — for regulatory reporting, financial statements, or major decisions — which is why CDE status is a small, deliberately selective subset of all documented data, not every column in the dictionary.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B confuses CDE status with ordinary dictionary documentation. Lesson 16 is explicit that 'not every documented column in the dictionary is a CDE' — a column can be perfectly documented, with a complete description, and still not qualify as critical if it doesn't meet the regulatory relevance, financial materiality, decision impact, or downstream reach criteria. CDE status is about the consequences of an error, not about documentation completeness.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about prioritizing CDEs with the impact/likelihood framework, per Lesson 17.
options: Impact reuses the four CDE criteria from Lesson 16 — regulatory, financial, decision, and downstream reach
Likelihood asks how probable it is the element is currently wrong, given its source and validation
A high-impact element is automatically the top priority regardless of its likelihood of error
A manually re-keyed field is generally considered more error-prone than one calculated deterministically from a reliable source
Once an organization identifies forty CDEs, prioritization becomes unnecessary since they're all already flagged as critical
questions.explain: Impact reuses Lesson 16's four criteria, and likelihood is about how probable an error actually is given the element's source and validation — a manually re-keyed field is riskier than a deterministically calculated one. A high-impact element isn't automatically top priority if its likelihood of error is low (TaxRate, sourced from a single validated table, ranks below OrderTotal despite comparable impact). And prioritization becomes more necessary, not less, once an organization has more CDEs than it can govern with equal intensity — exactly the scenario the lesson says prioritization solves.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on a documented CDE record, the ________ is the person notified immediately when that specific element fails a quality check — distinct from the element's general owner, because a CDE failure often needs a faster response than routine maintenance.
questions.explain: Lesson 18 names this the escalation contact — one of the four additional fields a CDE record carries beyond a standard dictionary entry, specifically because a CDE failure often demands a faster response than routine dictionary maintenance.

questions.prompt: Match each additional CDE record field to what it actually captures, per Lesson 18.
right: A direct link to the actual data quality rule that checks this element
A short description of how the element moves from its source to where it's consumed
Who gets notified immediately when this element fails a quality check
The one authoritative system this element originates from, named explicitly
questions.explain: Source system of record names the one authoritative origin system explicitly. Validation rule reference links directly to the actual data quality rule. Lineage summary describes how the element travels from source to consumption. Escalation contact is who's notified immediately on a failure, distinct from the general owner.

questions.prompt: An auditor reviewing a bank's BCBS 239 compliance asks to see the risk-reporting CDE list. The bank's data team says 'our senior analyst just knows which fields matter.' Per Lesson 19, how does this hold up under audit?
options: It fails — BCBS 239 requires a documented, governed CDE list with assigned ownership and lineage, not knowledge held informally by one person
It's acceptable, since BCBS 239 only cares about the final reported numbers, not how the underlying data is tracked
It's acceptable, as long as the senior analyst is willing to answer questions verbally during the audit
It fails only if the bank is a US-based institution; BCBS 239 doesn't apply to banks headquartered elsewhere
questions.explain: Lesson 19 is explicit that a regulatory audit checks whether a documented CDE list actually exists — 'not informally known by one person, but written down and governed' — with a named, accountable owner and evidence of lineage and validation. A bank that can't produce that documentation is failing BCBS 239's requirement directly, regardless of how knowledgeable any individual analyst is.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 20, why is a data catalog described as an 'integration point' rather than a fourth standalone metadata repository alongside the glossary, dictionary, and lineage tools?
options: Because a well-designed catalog pulls business definitions from the glossary, structural metadata from the dictionary, and lineage from pipeline tools into one searchable surface, rather than requiring anyone to re-enter what's already documented elsewhere
Because catalogs are legally required to connect to at least three other systems before they can be used
Because a catalog can only display data, never store any metadata of its own
Because the glossary and dictionary are retired once a catalog is built
questions.explain: Lesson 20 explains that a poorly designed catalog just adds a fourth place metadata has to be separately maintained, worsening the repository sprawl problem from Lesson 5. A well-designed one instead reads from the existing glossary, dictionary, and lineage tools and presents it all as one searchable surface, resolving the sprawl rather than adding to it.

questions.prompt: Select every one of the four catalog capabilities Lesson 21 names as separating a genuinely useful catalog from a glorified spreadsheet.
options: Full-text search across both business and technical metadata
Faceted filtering by attributes like owner, system, or status
Relationship navigation, like clicking from a glossary term to the dictionary entries that implement it
Usage-based ranking that surfaces actively-queried results above untouched ones
A requirement that every search return exactly one result, to avoid overwhelming the user
questions.explain: Lesson 21 names exactly four capabilities: full-text search across both metadata types, faceted filtering, relationship navigation between linked entries, and usage-based ranking. Forcing every search to return exactly one result isn't one of them — narrowing results happens through faceted filtering, not by artificially capping result counts.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: of the four metadata quality dimensions in Lesson 23 (coverage, freshness, correctness, consistency), ________ asks whether a description actually matches what the column contains right now — directly the descriptive-drift problem from Lesson 15.
questions.explain: Correctness is Lesson 23's dimension for whether a description still matches reality right now — the same descriptive-drift failure Lesson 15 described, which is dangerous precisely because it fails silently rather than showing up as an obviously empty field.

questions.prompt: Match each catalog adoption barrier to its corresponding tactic, per Lesson 24.
right: Actively announce it where people already look, rather than passively publishing and hoping for discovery
Integrate the catalog into existing workflows, like embedding a search widget in the BI tool people already use daily
Launch with a smaller, genuinely high-quality scope rather than a comprehensive but spotty one
questions.explain: Habit is countered by embedding the catalog into tools people already open daily. Trust is built by launching a smaller, consistently reliable scope rather than a comprehensive but spotty one. Visibility is addressed by actively announcing the catalog where people already look, not just passively publishing it.

questions.prompt: The Hartwell Logistics case study in Lesson 25 applies this course chapter by chapter to fix a recurring 'on-time delivery' disagreement. Put these chapter-by-chapter actions in the order the case study applies them.
items: Recognize that 'on-time delivery' has tangled business, technical, and operational metadata with no shared standard or lifecycle discipline
Start a scoped glossary effort for the delivery-performance domain and write one definition that passes the four-part test
Document the actual column, pulling structural facts from INFORMATION_SCHEMA and attaching the glossary-linked description
Score the element against the CDE criteria and add the elevated documentation a Critical Data Element requires
Publish the standardized definition into the catalog and apply adoption tactics so people actually use it
questions.explain: The case study follows this course's own chapter order: Chapter 1 diagnoses the tangled, unstandardized metadata; Chapter 2 scopes a glossary effort and writes a four-part-test definition; Chapter 3 documents the real column from the schema; Chapter 4 recognizes it as a CDE and adds the elevated documentation that status requires; Chapter 5 publishes it into the catalog and deliberately drives adoption, which is what finally gets all three teams referencing the same definition.

questions.prompt: A catalog entry for dbo.Customer.IsActiveFlag has its description field completely empty. A second catalog entry has a description that reads 'True when customer purchased in the last 90 days' — but the business redefined 'active' to 60 days eight months ago and nobody updated it. Per Lesson 23, which failure is more dangerous, and why?
options: The second one — a correctness failure fails silently, looking complete and trustworthy while actually being wrong, whereas the empty field is an obvious, easy-to-spot coverage failure
The first one — an empty field always causes a visible system error, while a wrong description never does
They're equally dangerous, since both are examples of the same quality dimension
Neither is dangerous, since catalog entries are only used for casual browsing, never for real decisions
questions.explain: Lesson 23 is explicit that the two failures leave a user with false confidence in different ways — the empty field (a coverage failure) fails obviously and is easy to spot, while the stale-but-present description (a correctness failure) looks complete and is actually wrong, which is far more dangerous precisely because nothing visibly signals the problem.

questions.prompt: A catalog is built entirely from automated scanning, with no manual curation layer. Per Lesson 22, what does this catalog actually give users?
options: Technically comprehensive entries that are practically useless for business users — it can say a column is an INT, but not what it means or who owns it
A catalog that is identical in usefulness to one built with both scanning and curation, since the technical facts are the hard part
No entries at all, since scanning alone cannot populate a catalog
Entries with business definitions but no structural details like data types or row counts
questions.explain: Lesson 22 is explicit that scanning guarantees coverage but not meaning — a scan-only catalog is technically comprehensive (it can tell you a column's type and row count) and completely useless for business users, since it never captures ownership, business context, or glossary links, which only manual curation by a steward can add.
